The Council of Economic Advisers (CEA), within the Executive Office of the President, seeks a Health Economist to serve as the Council's senior economist for health on a one-year assignment. CEA provides the President with objective economic analysis and advice across domestic and international economic policy and prepares the annual Economic Report of the President.
The economist will design and conduct original economic analysis on healthcare policy — including healthcare financing, Medicare and Medicaid, insurance markets, pharmaceutical pricing and innovation, provider competition, and public health — and translate that analysis into concise, decision-ready advice for the Chairman, the Members, and the President's senior policy advisors and councils.
A defining focus of the position is the economics of the essential-medicines supply chain: assessing options to reshore production to the United States and friend-shore it to allied and partner nations for active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), key starting materials (KSMs), and critical medical products; reducing dependence on concentrated or geographically vulnerable foreign sources; and sustaining domestic manufacturing capacity, private investment, and the sector's technological and intellectual-property leadership. Position 1-3 full-time Post-Doctoral Associate positions, available starting in 2027 for 1-3 years (one-year positions are only available to applicants who have secured a subsequent appointment as an assistant professor, research scientist, or research economist)
Employer MIT FutureTech (futuretech.mit.edu) at:
MIT Sloan School of Management’s Initiative on the Digital Economy (IDE) and MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL)
Location Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA
Job Description Dr. Neil Thompson, Director of MIT FutureTech, seeks to hire up to three Postdoctoral Associates, with a preference for candidates whose research connects to at least one of the following areas:
(i) AI progress and timelines Rapid advances in AI capabilities have raised both excitement and uncertainty about the pace of future progress. Projections of when specific milestones (e.g., human level performance on complex tasks, widespread deployment of autonomous systems) will be reached differ significantly across researchers, research fields, and industry. This project area seeks to rigorously characterize historical and current trends in AI development and to model plausible future trajectories. Relevant work might include: quantitative measurement of scaling laws and other empirical regularities in algorithmic improvement; analysis of hardware, energy, data, and talent constraints that could accelerate or limit progress; economic, regulatory, and geopolitical factors shaping investment and research concentration; scenario modeling of short-, medium, and long term capability benchmarks; and assessment of feedback loops between AI deployment and further innovation. Insights generated should help clarify realistic timelines, identify key uncertainties, and inform strategic decisions by firms, governments, and society at large regarding preparedness and governance of advanced AI systems. Examples of previous work from the lab in this area include: Algorithmic Progress; Last Mile.
(ii) The Effect of AI on Science AI has driven advancements in many scientific fields, such as drug discovery, materials science, protein folding, or weather prediction. It is also well known that scientific progress is a key engine for economic growth. This project focuses on understanding the impact of AI on science and the resulting economic consequences. Key topics we aim to address include quantifying the impact of AI on scientific progress and economic growth, the extent to which AI will augment and/or change the R&D production function, and the implications of AI-driven R&D for researchers, firms, and policy. Examples of previous work from the lab in this area include: Influence of Industry; AI-augmented R&D.
(iii) Future of Work and the Labor Market Effects of AI and ICT What are the (global) labor market implications of new technologies, such as AI and ICT? Do workers within firms benefit from IT improvements and the adoption of AI? If so, which workers specifically benefit, and which are adversely affected through slower wage growth or job displacement? How quickly will jobs be replaced or augmented by AI? Are workers (or individual tasks) complements or substitutes to AI and ICT? Furthermore, how does overall labor demand change in response to advancements in AI? We aim to address these and related questions by leveraging detailed firm-worker-level data from administrative sources (e.g., census data), publicly available task-level data (e.g., ONET), and self-collected surveys. By studying these dynamics, our goal is to gain a deeper understanding of the future of work in the context of the rise of new technologies. Examples of previous work from the lab in this area include: Beyond AI Exposure; Expertise; Crashing waves vs. Rising Tides.
(iv) The Impact of AI on Industry and Firm Performance AI is widely recognized as having the potential to revolutionize industries and transform firms’ production processes. However, significant gaps remain in our understanding of how AI will affect firm and industry performance both within and across countries. In this project, we aim to develop novel measures of industry exposure to AI and compile data on AI adoption to investigate how AI shapes firm performance, productivity, and market power in national and international contexts. Key questions include identifying the key determinants of AI adoption; how AI affects firms’ market shares and productivity; how these changes influence competition and aggregate productivity; and whether cross-country differences in AI adoption and exposure will narrow or widen existing economic disparities. Examples of the lab’s previous work in this area include: IT and RTS.
In addition to researching these issues, the post-doc will be expected to become a team leader, supervising and mentoring younger students.
Qualifications • PhD or equivalent in economics or related field • Demonstrated expertise in computing / AI • Interest in working in an interdisciplinary lab with computer scientists and engineers • Strong data analysis skills, including statistical/econometric training • For some positions, experience working with U.S. census data would be a plus • Knowledge of relevant theoretical models • Proficiency with a modern programming language, e.g., Python, R • Solid English communication skills (verbal and written) • Desire and skill (e.g. organizational abilities) to work in teams
The post-doc’s primary appointment would be at the MIT Sloan School of Management, and would have a secondary appointment at the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab.
Salary $75,000 per year, plus benefits.

position.jp_full_text:
Princeton University is pleased to announce the call for applications to the Fung Global Fellows Program at the Princeton Institute for International and Regional Studies (PIIRS). The program will select early-career scholars from around the world to be in residence at Princeton for an academic year and to engage in research and discussion around a common theme. The fellowships will be awarded to those employed outside the United States who have a faculty appointment or a professional research appointment, and they will be expected to return to their positions at the conclusion of the fellowship.
Democratic governance faces mounting pressure around the world. The rise of populist movements, declining trust in institutions, polarization, disinformation, and democratic backsliding (including in democracies once considered as consolidated) have prompted renewed debate about whether democracy's ascendance in the late 20th century was more fragile than assumed. At the same time, democracies have proven resilient in unexpected ways through grassroots mobilization, institutional safeguards, judicial independence, and civic renewal, raising the question of what, precisely, allows some democratic systems to weather crisis while others erode or collapse.
During the 2027-28 academic year, the program theme will be "Democracy in Crisis?" We invite applications from scholars who study the challenges confronting democratic governance and/or the sources of democratic resilience. Projects might explore the drivers and dynamics of populism; the erosion of democratic norms and institutions; the role of media, technology, and disinformation in shaping political life; the relationship between economic inequality and democratic legitimacy; or the strategies through which citizens, civil society, and institutions have defended or renewed democratic practice. We are equally interested in work that interrogates the conceptual and normative foundations of democracy itself, what it means, who it serves, and how it has been imagined and contested across different political and cultural traditions.
Applicants may address any region of the world and can bring contemporary and/or historical perspectives to bear. We welcome scholars from across the humanities and social sciences.
Applicants must apply online at https://apply.interfolio.com/191685. Applications are due on November 16, 2026 (11:59 p.m. EST).
To be eligible, applicants must have received their Ph.D. (or equivalent) generally after September 1, 2017. Candidates who are currently enrolled in a Ph.D. program or employed as postdocs are not eligible to apply. Fellowships will be awarded on the strength of a candidate's proposed research project, the relationship of that project to the program's theme, the candidate's scholarly record, and their ability to contribute to the intellectual life of the program. For more information, see: https://funggfp.princeton.edu/applications.
The following items must be submitted by the applicant, in English, by November 16, 2026:
Cover letter (1.5 pages maximum) Curriculum Vitae (including publications) Research proposal (maximum of 3 pages, single spaced) One writing sample (article or book chapter, maximum of 50 pages) The names and email addresses for three referees, who will be contacted automatically by the online application system with an invitation to upload their letter of recommendation to the system by the application deadline.
Should an offer be made, successful candidates who hold faculty appointments or professional research appointments will be required to submit an official letter from their current employer affirming that they would be permitted to accept the offer and to spend the academic year at Princeton University.The work location for these positions is in-person, on campus at Princeton University.

Position Summary
The Council of Economic Advisers seeks a Staff Economist to lead supply chain analysis across the nation's most critical and strategically vulnerable sectors. The role combines applied microeconomic and trade analysis with hands-on supply chain mapping—tracing where critical goods and their upstream inputs actually originate—and modeling how economic, trade, and procurement tools can shift sourcing toward the United States and partner nations.
The portfolio spans four priority areas: pharmaceuticals (finished drugs, active pharmaceutical ingredients (APIs), and key starting materials (KSMs)); semiconductors (with an emphasis on legacy/mature-node "foundational" chips); batteries and drones (cells, components, and the unmanned aircraft supply base); and critical minerals (extraction and, critically, processing and refining). A common analytical toolkit applies across all four: identify single-source vulnerabilities, distinguish direct from indirect exposure, and design economic levers to diversify supply.
This is a high-impact position for an economist who can move fluently between rigorous quantitative work and concrete policy design, and who is comfortable briefing senior officials on time-sensitive questions. ________________________________________
Key Responsibilities
Supply chain mapping and dependency analysis (across all priority sectors)
Build and maintain an evidence base on where critical goods and their upstream inputs originate, identifying single-source and country-concentration risks. Distinguish extraction/assembly from the true chokepoints, which often sit midstream—e.g., mineral processing and refining, mature-node foundry capacity, cell and cathode/anode manufacturing, and API/KSM synthesis. Integrate data from customs and import records, HS/HTS-level trade flows, FDA establishment registrations, foundry capacity by node and geography, and commercial supply chain sources to quantify concentration (e.g., HHI, single-country shares) and map vulnerabilities. Develop criticality metrics (defense and clinical relevance, substitutability, shortage/disruption history) and resilience metrics (geographic diversification, domestic capacity, inventory, stockpiles).
Sector-specific focus areas
Pharmaceuticals: finished-drug, API, and KSM sourcing; shortage risk. Semiconductors: legacy/mature-node chips embedded in autos, defense systems, medical devices, appliances, and grid hardware; risks from non-market capacity expansion and price suppression. Batteries and drones: lithium-ion cells and components, cathode/anode and precursor materials, and the unmanned aircraft (UAS) supply base, including secure-component and trusted-supplier considerations. Critical minerals: rare earths, lithium, cobalt, nickel, graphite, gallium, germanium and similar.
Policy tool analysis
Model the cost, feasibility, and likely supply response of economic and procurement levers, including trade remedies, Buy American and domestic-content preferences and penalties, federal procurement preferences and restrictions, advance purchase and offtake commitments, stockpiling, and targeted onshoring/ally-shoring incentives. Estimate effects on prices, availability and shortage risk, domestic manufacturing investment, and downstream costs; assess budgetary impact, unintended consequences, and gaming risks. Conduct cost-benefit and trade-off analysis weighing resilience gains against consumer-price and fiscal effects.
Partner-country and friend-shoring strategy
Analyze opportunities to diversify supply with allied and partner nations, including the economic case for ally-shoring of upstream production and processing. Assess how trade preferences, joint procurement, coordinated incentives, and partnership frameworks could stand up trusted alternative suppliers and shared stockpiles.
Briefing and inter-agency work
Produce memos, charts, and briefing materials. Support inter-agency analysis with partners. ________________________________________
Qualifications
Required
Advanced degree in economics or a closely related quantitative field (PhD preferred; exceptional candidates with a master's and strong relevant experience considered). Demonstrated applied skills in microeconomics, industrial organization, and/or international trade. Strong empirical and data skills (e.g., Stata, R, or Python) and the ability to work with messy real-world trade, customs, regulatory, and industry datasets. Ability to translate technical analysis into clear, decision-ready writing for non-economist principals.- Capacity to work quickly and accurately under deadline pressure on sensitive policy questions.
Preferred
Familiarity with one or more priority sectors: pharmaceutical manufacturing and the API/KSM value chain; semiconductor manufacturing and the mature-node landscape; battery and UAS supply chains; or critical minerals extraction and processing. Knowledge of U.S. trade- and industrial-policy instruments. Experience with supply-chain, network, or concentration analysis. Prior government, think tank, or inter-agency experience.

The Institute of Population and Human Capital at Yonsei University invites applications for Postdoctoral Fellows. We welcome qualified candidates with a strong interest in population and human capital research.
Main Responsibilities Conduct independent and collaborative research in Health, Education, Population, Migration, Family, Vulnerable Populations, Inequality, Children, Aging, AI, and International Development. Analyze large-scale administrative datasets. Design, implement, and analyze large-scale Randomized Controlled Trials (RCTs). Support ongoing research and book projects. Mentor master’s students and assist in preparing teaching materials. Develop and lead independent research aligned with the Institute's priorities.
Postdoctoral Fellows will be matched with research topics suited to their expertise. Research will be conducted in collaboration with faculty members at Yonsei University, under the supervision of the Institute Director, Hyuncheol Bryant Kim.
Qualifications Ph.D. in Economics or a related field. Strong background in applied microeconomics. Experience working with large administrative datasets and/or RCTs is highly preferred.
Selection and Appointment Document screening followed by interviews. Flexible start date from January 2027 through September 1, 2027, with earlier availability preferred. Initial two-year appointment, with possible renewal for a third year.
